chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinanī, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who was unaware of entering the state of Ihram until he entered the Haram (sanctuary), what should he do? He said, 'He exits the Haram, then enters Ihram for Hajj.'

All these narrations indicate the obligation of Ihram, because the first report included a prohibition on crossing the Miqat (boundary) without Ihram, and the remaining reports indicate that whoever crosses it must return to the Miqat of his people if he is able to do so; if he is not able, he enters Ihram from where he is. If its obligation and emphasis as a duty were not established, this strictness would not have been applied, and its omission would have been permissible in all cases.
As for that which indicates the obligation of Talbiyah, it is what he narrated:

key_terms.التَّلْبِيَةِ: The recitation of 'Labbayk' (Here I am) during Hajj
key_terms.الْإِحْرَام: The ritual state of consecration for Hajj or Umrah
key_terms.الْحَرَم: The Sanctuary (specifically the sacred area of Mecca)
key_terms.الْمِيقَات: The designated boundary stations for entering Ihram

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim who crosses the Miqat boundary without entering Ihram?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi uses this narration from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani to demonstrate the obligatory nature (wajib) of Ihram by analyzing the logical implication of the strict penalty for crossing the Miqat without it. The text highlights the juristic principle that if a ritual were merely recommended, the requirement to return to the specific boundary would not be so rigorous, thereby confirming Ihram as a fundamental pillar of Hajj.
